title: pkix-path accepts CVE-2025-61727: a wildcard SAN evades dNSName name constraints
description:
x509-limbo's cve::cve-2025-61727 and cve::cve-2025-61727-nc-permits-variant both expect FAILURE and pkix-path passes them. Found by wiring expected_peer_name through the harness (PKIX-rnsv); before that the peer name was never checked, so the case could not be scored.

The chain:

  root -> ICA (nameConstraints: excluded bar.example.com) -> EE (SAN: *.example.com)

with the peer name bar.example.com requested.

Mechanism, confirmed in the code:

1. Path validation compares the literal SAN string *.example.com against the excluded subtree bar.example.com. It does not match -- *.example.com is not within bar.example.com as a string -- so the constraint is satisfied and the path is valid. grep for 'wildcard' across pkix-path/src/lib.rs finds only anyPolicy and one unrelated index comment: the dNSName constraint path has no wildcard awareness at all.

2. pkix-identity::verify_dns_name then matches the requested bar.example.com against the SAN *.example.com via dns_name_matches_pattern, which succeeds.

Net effect: an intermediate CA explicitly forbidden from certifying bar.example.com successfully issues a certificate that authenticates bar.example.com. Neither crate is wrong in isolation -- the composition is.

The permits variant is the same hole from the other side: ICA permitted only foo.example.com issues SAN *.example.com, which is broader than its permission, and the peer name foo.example.com is then accepted.

limbo's own description notes this sits in an ambiguity between RFC 5280 (constraints apply to subjects and SANs) and RFC 9525 (wildcard matching semantics): neither defines how constraints apply to a peer name when the SAN matches the peer name but not the constraint. Its stated expectation is that validators behave defensively and reject a chain where a subject name *might* match a peer name that would violate the constraint.

Recommended fix: bound the wildcard's coverage rather than its spelling. In the dNSName constraint check, treat *.example.com as the set of names it can authenticate, then

  - reject if that set intersects any excluded subtree, and
  - require that set to be a subset of the permitted subtrees.

That handles both testcases: *.example.com covers bar.example.com so it intersects the exclusion, and *.example.com is not a subset of foo.example.com so it fails the permission. It also fixes the class rather than the two cases, and keeps the decision inside path validation where the constraint set lives.

Alternative considered and dispreferred: re-check the concrete peer name against the chain's constraints after identity matching, at the pkix-chain layer. It answers the literal question but leaves pkix-path accepting the chain, so any consumer validating a path without going through that layer stays exposed.

This needs a decision before implementing, because being defensive here is stricter than RFC 5280 read literally and may reject certificates other validators accept: a CA with a narrow dNSName constraint that issues wildcard SANs is not obviously misissuance under a literal reading. The counter-argument is that the literal reading makes a name constraint unenforceable against exactly the certificate shape most used in practice.

Not a regression: pkix-path has always behaved this way. It became visible only once the harness started asking the identity question.
